description: The bar chart illustrates five distinct distribution patterns—labeled “Increasing,” “Uniform,” “Decreasing,” “Spindle,” and “Bottleneck”—each represented by a group of four vertical bars of varying heights, arranged horizontally across the chart. The horizontal axis categorizes these five patterns, while the vertical axis, though unlabeled, represents a relative magnitude or frequency scale, with bar heights visually indicating proportional values. In the “Increasing” pattern, bar heights rise progressively from left to right, starting low and peaking at the fourth bar. The “Uniform” pattern shows four bars of nearly identical height, indicating consistent values across all positions. The “Decreasing” pattern mirrors the “Increasing” one in reverse, with the tallest bar on the left and heights declining to the right. The “Spindle” pattern features a central peak, with the second and third bars taller than the first and fourth, forming a symmetric, bell-like shape. The “Bottleneck” pattern has the shortest bars in the middle (second and third positions), flanked by taller bars on the ends, creating a U-shaped profile. All bars are rendered in a uniform gray tone, with no color differentiation or numerical axis labels, emphasizing qualitative shape comparison over precise quantitative values. The chart appears to visually represent different architectural or parameter allocation strategies in the context of parameter-efficient fine-tuning, as suggested by the paper title.
